etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English policie, from Old French policie, pollicie and police, from Late Latin politia (“citizenship; government”), classical Latin polītīa (in Cicero), from Ancient Greek πολιτεία (politeía, “citizenship; polis, (city) state; government”), from πολίτης (polítēs, “citizen”). Compare police and polity.

definitions.definition: A principle of behaviour, conduct etc. thought to be desirable or necessary, especially as formally expressed by a government or other authoritative body. [from 15th c.]
A document describing such a policy.
Wise or advantageous conduct; prudence, formerly also with connotations of craftiness. [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: 1639, Thomas Fuller, “King Richard Taken Prisoner in Austria; Sold and Sent to the Emperour; Dearly Ransomed, Returneth Home”, in The Historie of the Holy Warre, Cambridge, Cambridgeshire:  […]  Thomas Buck, one of the printers to the Universitie of Cambridge [and sold by John Williams, London], →OCLC, book III, page 130:
quote.text: [H]e [Richard I of England] was diſcovered in an inne in Auſtria, becauſe he diſguiſed his perſon not his expenſes; ſo that the very policie of an hoſteſſe, finding his purſe ſo farre above his clothes, did detect him:  […]

quote.citation: 1813 January 27, [Jane Austen], chapter XI, in Pride and Prejudice: […], volume II, London:  […]  [George Sidney] for T[homas] Egerton, […], →OCLC, page 131:
quote.text: These bitter accusations might have been suppressed, had I with greater policy concealed my struggles, and flattered you into the belief of my being impelled by unqualified, unalloyed inclination;  […]

definitions.definition: (now rare) Specifically, political shrewdness or (formerly) cunning; statecraft. [from 15th c.]

quote.citation: c. 1589–1590 (date written), Christopher Marlo[we], edited by Tho[mas] Heywood, The Famous Tragedy of the Rich Iew of Malta. […], London:  […]  I[ohn] B[eale] for Nicholas Vavasour, […], published 1633, →OCLC, Act I:
quote.text: I, 'policie? that's their profession,And not simplicity, as they suggest.

quote.citation: 1946, Bertrand Russell, History of Western Philosophy, I.25:
quote.text: Whether he believed himself a god, or only took on the attributes of divinity from motives of policy, is a question for the psychologist, since the historical evidence is indecisive.

definitions.definition: (Scotland, now chiefly in the plural) The grounds of a large country house. [from 18th c.]

quote.citation: 1775, Samuel Johnson, A Journey to the Western Islands of Scotland section on Aberbrothick
quote.text: Now and then about a gentleman’s house stands a small plantation, which in Scotch is called a policy, but of these there are few, and those few all very young.

quote.citation: 1886 May 1 – July 31, Robert Louis Stevenson, Kidnapped, being Memoirs of the Adventures of David Balfour in the Year 1751: […], London; Paris: Cassell & Company, published 1886, →OCLC:
quote.text: There was but one thing happened worth narrating; and that is the visit I had of Robin Oig, one of the sons of the notorious Rob Roy. He was sought upon all sides on a charge of carrying a young woman from Balfron and marrying her (as was alleged) by force; yet he stepped about Balquhidder like a gentleman in his own walled policy.

quote.citation: 1955, Robin Jenkins, The Cone-Gatherers, Canongate, published 2012, page 36:
quote.text: Next morning was so splendid that as he walked through the policies towards the mansion house despair itself was lulled.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) The art of governance; political science. [14th–18th c.]

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i], pages 69–70:
quote.text: Liſt his diſcourse of Warre; and you ſhall heare / A fearefull Battaile rendred you in Muſique. / Turne him to any Cauſe of Pollicy, / The Gordian Knot of it he will vnlooſe, / Familiar as his Garter:  […]

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A set political system; civil administration. [15th–19th c.]

quote.citation: c. 1588–1593 (date written), [William Shakespeare], The Most Lamentable Romaine Tragedie of Titus Andronicus: […] (First Quarto), London:  […]  Iohn Danter, and are to be sold by Edward White & Thomas Millington, […], published 1594, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:
quote.text: Tis pollicie and ſtratageme must doo / That you affect, and ſo muſt you reſolue, / That what you cannot as you would atchiue, / You muſt perforce accompliſh as you may:  […]

quote.citation: c. 1580 (date written), Philippe Sidnei [i.e., Philip Sidney], “(please specify the folio)”, in [Fulke Greville; Matthew Gwinne; John Florio], editors, The Countesse of Pembrokes Arcadia [The New Arcadia], London:  […]  [John Windet] for William Ponsonbie, published 1590, →OCLC:
quote.text: I pray you (said he) honest men, what such right have you in me, as not to suffer me to doe with my self what I list? and what pollicie have you to bestow a benefite where it is counted an injury?

definitions.definition: (transitive) To regulate by laws; to reduce to order.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French police, from Italian polizza, from Medieval Latin apodissa (“receipt for money”), from Ancient Greek ἀπόδειξις (apódeixis, “proof, declaration”). Doublet of apodixis.
